claim: In the last mitotic division of the epidermal lineage in the ascidian embryo, the cells divide stereotypically along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: In the last mitotic division of the epidermal lineage in the ascidian embryo, the cells divide stereotypically along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from live imaging analysis presented in the manuscript, as well as previous reports cited (Ogura et al., 2011).

claim: During interphase, a unique membrane structure invaginates from the posterior to the centre of the cell, in a microtubule-dependent manner.
source: During interphase, we found that a unique membrane structure invaginates from the posterior to the centre of the cell, in a microtubule-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing the membrane invagination and by experimental data showing that nocodazole treatment (which depolymerizes microtubules) blocks invagination formation.

claim: The invagination projects toward centrioles on the apical side of the nucleus and associates with one of them.
source: The invagination projects toward centrioles on the apical side of the nucleus and associates with one of them.
evidence: This claim is supported by SBF-SEM imaging data showing the invagination approaching centrioles and by live imaging showing the spatial relationship between invaginations and centrosomes.

claim: A cilium forms on the posterior side of the cell and its basal body remains associated with the invagination.
source: Further, a cilium forms on the posterior side of the cell and its basal body remains associated with the invagination.
evidence: This claim is supported by SBF-SEM data showing cilia near centrioles associated with invaginations, immunostaining data showing posterior cilium localization, and live imaging with Arl13b-GFP showing cilia associated with invaginations.

claim: A laser ablation experiment suggests that the invagination is under tensile force and promotes the posterior positioning of the centrosome.
source: A laser ablation experiment suggests that the invagination is under tensile force and promotes the posterior positioning of the centrosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from laser ablation experiments showing rapid regression of the invagination after cutting, indicating tensile force.

claim: The orientation of the invaginations is coupled with the polarized dynamics of centrosome movements and the orientation of cell division.
source: Finally, we showed that the orientation of the invaginations is coupled with the polarized dynamics of centrosome movements and the orientation of cell division.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing correlation between invagination direction and centrosome axis, and by Dishevelled knockdown experiments showing that disruption of directional invaginations correlates with randomized spindle orientation.

claim: The orientation of the mitotic division axis controls tissue morphogenesis and cell fate determination.
source: The orientation of the mitotic division axis has been proposed to control tissue morphogenesis as well as cell fate determination, thus playing an important role in shaping embryonic forms (Lu and Johnston, 2013; Moorhouse and Burgess, 2014; Siller and Doe, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanism determining the orientation of the mitotic spindle has been extensively studied in both cultured and embryonic cells and precise molecular processes are well understood.
source: The mechanism determining the orientation of the mitotic spindle has been extensively studied in both cultured and embryonic cells and precise molecular processes are well understood (Bell et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2010; Delaval et al., 2011; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012; Woolner and Papalopulu, 2012; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One strategy to achieve spindle orientation is the control of centrosome dynamics.
source: One strategy to achieve this is the control of centrosome dynamics.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about spindle orientation mechanisms.

claim: Centrosome works as a microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells and consists of a pair of mother and daughter centrioles, which are distinct in both structure and age.
source: Centrosome works as a microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells and consists of a pair of mother and daughter centrioles, which are distinct in both structure and age (Azimzadeh and Bornens, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about centrosome structure.

claim: Following duplication and migration, the two centrosomes become aligned to serve as spindle poles during mitosis.
source: Following duplication and migration, the two centrosomes become aligned to serve as spindle poles during mitosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about centrosome behavior during cell division.

claim: The axis of centrosome alignment is frequently consistent with mitotic spindle orientation unless additional constraints such as cell shape exist to alter the spindle orientation.
source: Thus, the axis of centrosome alignment is frequently consistent with mitotic spindle orientation unless additional constraints such as cell shape exist to alter the spindle orientation (Gibson et al., 2011; Minc et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Specific mother-daughter centrosome inheritance coupled with asymmetric cell division is a highly conserved phenomenon.
source: Specific mother-daughter centrosome inheritance coupled with asymmetric cell division is a highly conserved phenomenon (Yamashita, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In budding yeast, the 'old' spindle pole body corresponding to the mother centrosome, segregates into the bud.
source: It has been first reported in budding yeast that the 'old' spindle pole body corresponding to the mother centrosome, segregates into the bud (Pereira et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila male germline cells, membrane localized Apc2 and Bazooka, associated with E-cadherin, tethers one centrosome adjacent to the hub.
source: In male germline cells, membrane localized Adenomatous polyposis coli 2 (Apc2) and the Drosophila Par-3 homolog, Bazooka, associated with E-cadherin, tethers one centrosome adjacent to the niche, called the hub, and consequently ensures spindle orientation and asymmetric stem cell division (Inaba et al., 2015a; Yamashita et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila male germline cells, it is the mother centrosome with stable astral microtubules which is anchored near the hub.
source: In male germline cells, it is the mother centrosome with stable astral microtubules which is anchored near the hub (Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts, the centrosome with the higher MTOC activity remains in the neuroblast following asymmetric cell division.
source: In neuroblasts, the centrosome with the higher MTOC activity remains in the neuroblast following asymmetric cell division (Rebollo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts, it is the daughter centrosome that is retained in the stem cell, in contrast to the male germ line.
source: In contrast to the male germ line, it is the daughter centrosome that is retained in the stem cell (Conduit and Raff, 2010; Januschke et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrobin, associated with the daughter centrosome, was found to be responsible for oriented cell division in Drosophila neuroblasts.
source: Centrobin, associated with the daughter centrosome, was found to be responsible for this oriented cell division (Januschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In both Drosophila male germline and neuroblast systems, the centrosome with a higher MTOC activity is less motile and is inherited by the stem cell.
source: In both cell systems, the centrosome with a higher MTOC activity is less motile and is inherited by the stem cell (Pelletier and Yamashita, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The centrosome has an important role in cilia formation.
source: In addition to a role in spindle orientation, the centrosome also has an important role in cilia formation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about centrosome function.

claim: During ciliogenesis, the mother centriole converts into the basal body in a quiescent (G0 phase) or interphase (G1 phase) cell to nucleate a primary cilium.
source: During ciliogenesis, the mother centriole converts into the basal body in a quiescent (G0 phase) or interphase (G1 phase) cell to nucleate a primary cilium.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ciliogenesis.

claim: Following re-entry or progression of the cell cycle, the primary cilium is disassembled and the basal body/mother centriole is reused for mitotic spindle formation.
source: Following re-entry or progression of the cell cycle, the primary cilium is disassembled and the basal body/mother centriole is reused for mitotic spindle formation (Kobayashi and Dynlacht, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ascidians belong to the phylum Tunicata, a sister group of the vertebrates.
source: In this study, we use embryos of ascidian, belonging to the phylum Tunicata, a sister group of the vertebrates (Satoh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Ascidian embryos are ideally suited to study mechanisms of cell division because of their invariant cleavage pattern and the small number of cells that form their bodies.
source: Ascidian embryos are ideally suited to study mechanisms of cell division because of their invariant cleavage pattern and the small number of cells that form their bodies (Conklin, 1905; Nishida, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pattern of cell division is highly conserved among different ascidian species.
source: The pattern of cell division is highly conserved among different ascidian species (Conklin, 1905; Lemaire et al., 2008; Zalokar and Sardet, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Almost all epidermal cells cleave along the anterior-posterior (A–P) axis at the last (11th) division when the Ciona embryo starts shaping into a tadpole larval form.
source: It was previously reported that almost all epidermal cells cleave along the anterior-posterior (A–P) axis at the last (11th) division when the Ciona embryo starts shaping into a tadpole larval form (Ogura et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: The perpendicular shift of the cell division axis during successive rounds of cell division is thought to result from a 90° translocation of the duplicated centrosomes around the nucleus to the opposite directions (Sach's rule).
source: The perpendicular shift of the cell division axis during successive rounds of cell division is thought to result from a 90° translocation of the duplicated centrosomes around the nucleus to the opposite directions (Sach's rule) (Mardin and Schiebel, 2012; Strome, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The alternating 90° shift of the division axis tends to follow the long-axis rule based on cell shape (Hertwig's rule).
source: This alternating 90° shift of the division axis tends to follow the long-axis rule based on cell shape (Hertwig's rule) (Hertwig, 1984; Minc et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Almost all epidermal cells divide along the A–P axis at the last (11th) division as confirmed by live imaging analysis.
source: With live imaging analysis of epidermal cell division, we confirmed that almost all epidermal cells divide along the A–P axis at the last (11th) division as reported previously (Ogura et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data presented in the manuscript and by citation to previous literature.

claim: The oriented cell division at the 11th cycle occurs regardless of the cell shape and whether the 10th cell division occurred along the A–P or M-L axis.
source: This oriented cell division occurs regardless of the cell shape and whether the 10th cell division occurred along the A–P or M-L axis (Figure 1A–C, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C and Video 1.

claim: During the 11th (but not the 10th) cell cycle, the nucleus of the epidermal cells gradually shifts toward the posterior side.
source: Additionally, we found, during the 11th (but not the 10th) cell cycle, that the nucleus of the epidermal cells gradually shifts toward the posterior side (Figure 1D,E and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E and Video 1.

claim: A unique membrane structure (invagination) forms in almost all of the epidermal cells specifically during the interphase of the last (11th) division cycle.
source: We found a unique structure (membrane invagination) that formed in almost all of the epidermal cells specifically during the interphase of the last (11th) division cycle (Figure 2A,B, magenta and blue arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The invaginating membrane does not adopt a stable, solid form, but rather appears to be a highly dynamic filamentous structure.
source: Time-lapse observations of cells that had committed to cell division revealed that the invaginating membrane did not adopt a stable, solid form, but rather appeared to be a highly dynamic filamentous structure (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 2.

claim: The invaginations are not an artefact of a specific protein or GFP staining itself, as confirmed by using memGFP and FM4-64.
source: To confirm the structure of the invaginating membranes, we used another membrane binding probe using a domain of c-Ha-Ras, memGFP (Morita et al., 2012) or membrane-staining fluorescent dye, FM4-64 (Figure 2C), which demonstrated that the invaginations were not an artefact of a specific protein or GFP staining itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C using alternative labeling methods.

claim: The filamentous structures are located near the apical surface approximately 1.5 μm beneath the apical membrane.
source: The filamentous structures are located near the apical surface approximately 1.5 μm beneath the apical membrane (base: 1.33 ± 0.56 µm, tip: 0.98 ± 0.37 µm n = 71, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The length of the invaginations changed over time, ranging from roughly one-third to half of the cell diameter (2.0–5.0 μm).
source: The length of the invaginations changed over time, ranging from roughly one-third to half of the cell diameter (2.0–5.0 μm) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Some cells that formed a vertex with posterior cells had two or more invaginations.
source: Interestingly, some cells that formed a vertex with posterior cells had two or more invaginations (Figure 2B, magenta arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most of the invaginations projected from the posterior or lateral side toward the anterior.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that most of the invaginations projected from the posterior or lateral side toward the anterior (Figure 2F), at a nearly perpendicular angle to the cell membrane (Figure 2G), although transient, randomly projected filamentous membranes were also observed (See Videos 6 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: The membrane structure forms near the apical cortex and elongates along the A-P axis.
source: These results suggest that the membrane structure forms near the apical cortex and elongates along the A-P axis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the imaging data showing the location and orientation of invaginations.

claim: All of the invaginations disappeared just before spindle formation became visible.
source: All of the invaginations disappeared just before spindle formation became visible, suggesting that the formation of the invagination is temporally regulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: The invaginations were observed without exception during the interphase of the 11th cell cycle in epidermal cells.
source: In fact, the invaginations were observed without exception during the interphase of the 11th cell cycle in epidermal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic observation of epidermal cells.

claim: SBF-SEM observations showed fragmented membrane structures directed toward the centrioles.
source: In a series of several hundred sections, we observed fragmented membrane structures directed toward the centrioles (Figure 3A, blue arrows, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by SBF-SEM imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: 3D reconstructions from serial sections showed the tip of the invagination approaching the centrioles as if to capture the organelle.
source: Notably, 3D reconstructions from serial sections (Figure 3B, Videos 4 and 5) showed the tip of the invagination approaching the centrioles as if to capture the organelle.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 3B and Videos 4 and 5.

claim: SEM images showed that the invaginations were formed of a double-bilayer plasma membrane and that adjacent posterior cell membrane also contributed to this structure.
source: SEM images showed that the invaginations were formed of a double-bilayer plasma membrane and that adjacent posterior cell membrane also contributed to this structure (Figure 3A, Videos 3–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEM imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Videos 3-5.

claim: At the border between two differently labelled cells, the invaginating membranes were labelled with both green and red fluorescence, indicating that the layers of the invaginating membrane were derived from both of the neighbouring cells.
source: At the border between two differently labelled cells, the invaginating membranes were labelled with both green and red fluorescence, indicating that the layers of the invaginating membrane were derived from the both of the neighbouring cells (Figure 3C, white arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color labeling experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interphase microtubule array was aligned with the A-P axis with its nucleation site localised at the posterior side.
source: We found that the interphase microtubule array was aligned with the A-P axis with its nucleation site localised at the posterior side, indicating that a stable MTOC was positioned to the posterior of the cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data using ensconsin-tdTomato to label microtubules.

claim: Before the formation of the invagination at the early interphase of the 11th cell cycle, EB3-labelled centrosomes were located beneath the apical surface of the epidermal cells.
source: Before the formation of the invagination at the early interphase of the 11th cell cycle, EB3-labelled centrosomes were located beneath the apical surface of the epidermal cells (Figure 4B, white arrowheads and Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Video 7.

claim: The invaginations appeared to extend toward highly concentrated EB3-mCherry signals over time.
source: These analyses showed that the invaginations appeared to extend toward highly concentrated EB3-mCherry signals over time (Figure 4C, 33'–79').
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The invagination and the centrosome remain associated during posterior displacement.
source: Importantly, the invagination and the centrosome remain associated during posterior displacement.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: During the 10th division cycle, centrosomes were distributed equally along the A-P axis of epidermal cells.
source: Although during the 10th division cycle, centrosomes were distributed equally along the A-P axis of epidermal cells (Figure 4D), in the 11th division cycle following the emergence of the membrane invagination, the distribution of centrosome positioning was strongly biased to the posterior of the cell (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the 11th division cycle following the emergence of the membrane invagination, the distribution of centrosome positioning was strongly biased to the posterior of the cell.
source: Although during the 10th division cycle, centrosomes were distributed equally along the A-P axis of epidermal cells (Figure 4D), in the 11th division cycle following the emergence of the membrane invagination, the distribution of centrosome positioning was strongly biased to the posterior of the cell (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: By the time the invagination disappeared, the centrosome had duplicated; the two centrosomes then migrated asymmetrically until they were aligned with the axis of invagination.
source: By the time the invagination disappeared, the centrosome had duplicated; the two centrosomes then migrated asymmetrically until they were aligned with the axis of invagination (Figure 4C, white brackets in 79').
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The posterior-most centrosome migrated a shorter distance than the anterior one in the 11th division cycle, while this is not the case in the previous cell cycle.
source: Indeed, our quantitative analysis indicated that the posterior-most centrosome migrated a shorter distance than the anterior one in the 11th division cycle, while this is not the case in the previous cell cycle (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The migrated centrosomes were well-aligned along the axis of membrane invagination.
source: The analysis revealed that the migrated centrosomes were well-aligned along the axis of membrane invagination (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Serial SBF-SEM sections revealed that primary cilia were located near the centrioles associated with the invaginations.
source: Interestingly, serial SBF-SEM sections revealed that primary cilia were located near the centrioles associated with the invaginations (Figure 5A and Video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by SBF-SEM imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Video 9.

claim: Posterior cilium positioning was highly reminiscent of the posterior centrosome positioning.
source: Posterior cilium positioning was highly reminiscent of the posterior centrosome positioning (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of cilium and centrosome positioning data.

claim: Almost all cilia are associated with invaginations (97.8%, 221/226 cells in three embryos).
source: Live imaging of a GFP-tagged ciliary protein, ADP-ribosylation factor-like (ARL) family of small GTPases, Arl13b (Duldulao et al., 2009; Paridaen et al., 2013), showed that almost all cilia are associated with invaginations (97.8%, 221/226 cells in three embryos, Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All Arl13b-GFP labelled structures disappeared in the mitotic phase (n = 165 cells).
source: All Arl13b-GFP labelled structures disappeared in the mitotic phase (n = 165 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of Arl13b-GFP labeled cells.

claim: The invagination tip comes in closer proximity to the basal body derived from the mother centriole than to the daughter centriole (9/10 invaginations).
source: Measuring the distance between the tip of invagination and two centrioles (basal body and daughter) in 3D images reconstructed from SBF-SEM sections revealed that the invagination tip comes in closer proximity to the basal body derived from the mother centriole (Kobayashi and Dynlacht, 2011) than to the daughter centriole (9/10 invaginations) (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from 3D reconstructed SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The basal body as well as the mother centriole are targets of the invagination.
source: These results suggest that the basal body as well as the mother centriole are targets of the invagination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proximity measurements showing invaginations approach the basal body/mother centriole more closely than the daughter centriole.

claim: Microtubule depolymerisation with nocodazole blocked the formation of invaginations completely.
source: Microtubule depolymerisation with nocodazole blocked the formation of invaginations completely (Figure 7B), indicating that MTOC activity induces the invaginations and that, in turn, the invaginations relocate the MTOC to the posterior of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nocodazole treatment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A treatment of embryos with cytochalasin, which perturbs actin polymerisation, increased the number of invaginations, which now originated from all lateral plasma membrane domains.
source: On the other hand, a treatment of embryos with cytochalasin, which perturbs actin polymerisation, increased the number of invaginations, which now originated from all lateral plasma membrane domains (Figure 7A–C and Video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cytochalasin treatment shown in Figure 7A-C and Video 10.

claim: The tubular membrane structure of ascidian epidermal cells depends on microtubule function, reminiscent of the 'nanotubes' described in Drosophila male germ cells.
source: Thus, the tubular membrane structure of ascidian epidermal cells depends on microtubule function, reminiscent of the 'nanotubes' described in Drosophila male germ cells (Inaba et al., 2015b), rather than the actin-based membrane tubes described in other systems (ex. some cytonemes and tunneling nanotubes) (Gerdes and Carvalho, 2008; Hsiung et al., 2005; Rustom et al., 2004; Sanders et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results showing microtubule dependence and comparison with structures described in cited literature.

claim: Drosophila microtubule-based nanotubes (MT-nanotubes) are filled with microtubules.
source: Drosophila microtubule-based nanotubes (MT-nanotubes) are filled with microtubules (Inaba et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: During live imaging analyses, microtubules were not observed within the membrane invaginations.
source: During the course of live imaging analyses, we did not observe microtubules within the membrane invaginations.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from live imaging experiments.

claim: The plus end of the microtubule labeled with EB3-mCherry reached to the tip of the invagination.
source: By contrast, we often observed that the plus end of the microtubule labeled with EB3-mCherry reached to the tip of the invagination (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Serial-TEM observation showed abundant microtubules between the tip of invagination and the basal body, but no microtubules were observed within the invagination itself.
source: Further, we explored the topological relationship between the membrane invagination and microtubules by serial transmission electron microscopy (serial-TEM) observation (Figure 7E, Video 11). In serial-TEM, the membrane invaginations were visualized as double bilayer fragments (Figure 7Ea–f) extending toward the basal body (Figure 7Eh–k). Abundant microtubules were also observed between the tip of invagination and the basal body (Figure 7Ef–h), but no microtubules were observed within the invagination itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-TEM imaging data shown in Figure 7E and Video 11.

claim: The membrane invagination in ascidian epidermal cell is distinct from microtubule-filled nanotubes although both tubular structures are sensitive to microtubule depolymerization.
source: These results indicate that the membrane invagination in ascidian epidermal cell is distinct from microtubule-filled nanotubes although both tubular structures are sensitive to microtubule depolymerization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of microtubule distribution in ascidian invaginations versus Drosophila nanotubes, despite both being microtubule-dependent.

claim: The membrane invagination may associate with the centrosome via microtubules.
source: Our results also indicate that the membrane invagination may associate with the centrosome via microtubules.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of microtubules between the invagination tip and centrosome, and the microtubule-dependence of invagination formation.

claim: The end of the cut edge of the invaginations regressed immediately to the basal position after laser ablation, suggesting that the invaginations are normally under tension.
source: Interestingly, the end of the cut edge of the invaginations regressed immediately to the basal position, suggesting that the invaginations are normally under tension (Figure 8A, Video 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Video 12.

claim: The longer invaginations had a tendency to regress more rapidly after laser ablation.
source: In the series of laser ablation experiments (Figure 8B), we noted that the longer invaginations had a tendency to regress more rapidly (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the initial length of invaginations and both average and max speed of regression (recoiling).
source: The results show a positive correlation between the initial length and both average and max speed of regression (recoiling).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of laser ablation data.

claim: When one of two invaginations that cooperatively support a single centrosome was cut, a significant recoil occurred toward the intact (uncut) invagination.
source: When we cut one of two invaginations that cooperatively support a single centrosome, a significant recoil occurred toward the intact (uncut) invagination (Video 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experimental data shown in Video 13.

claim: The centrosome was balanced by two invaginations that generate pulling forces.
source: This finding strongly suggests that the centrosome was balanced by two invaginations that generate pulling forces.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cutting one invagination causes recoil toward the intact invagination.

claim: Soon (15 min) after the cutting, the plasma membrane re-invaginated toward the centrosome.
source: Interestingly, soon (15 min) after the cutting, we found that the plasma membrane re-invaginated toward the centrosome (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging after laser ablation shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Depletion of Dishevelled (Dsh) by injection of antisense morpholino oligo (MO) resulted in a radial formation of multiple membrane invaginations.
source: To disrupt the PCP pathway, we depleted Dishevelled (Dsh) (Hotta et al., 2003; Theisen et al., 1994; Wallingford and Habas, 2005), a core component of PCP, by injection of antisense morpholino oligo (MO). This resulted in a radial formation of multiple membrane invaginations (Figure 9A,B, Figure 10A, blue arrows, and Video 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Dsh MO injection shown in Figures 9 and 10 and Video 14.

claim: Disruption of directional membrane invaginations was strongly correlated with randomization of mitotic spindle orientation.
source: Disruption of directional membrane invaginations was strongly correlated with randomization of mitotic spindle orientation (Figure 9A,B, Figure 10A and Video 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Dsh knockdown experiments shown in Figures 9 and 10 and Video 14.

claim: Co-injection of Dsh mRNA with Dsh MO rescued both the direction of invaginations and cell division orientation along the A-P axis.
source: Co-injection of Dsh mRNA with Dsh MO rescued both the direction of invaginations and cell division orientation along the A-P axis (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The posterior distribution of the invaginations is tightly associated with the direction of mitotic divisions.
source: These results suggest that the posterior distribution of the invaginations is tightly associated with the direction of mitotic divisions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between invagination direction and spindle orientation observed in Dsh knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: The nuclei were distributed around the center of the cells with the omni-directional invaginations, as opposed to the posterior localisation observed in the cells with directional invaginations.
source: We also found that the nuclei were distributed around the center of the cells with the omni-directional invaginations, as opposed to the posterior localisation observed in the cells with directional invaginations (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The centrosomes were positioned in the center of the cells with the radial formation of invaginations.
source: Moreover, the centrosomes were also positioned in the center of the cells with the radial formation of invaginations (Figure 10A; Omni-directional 86', Figure 10C and Video 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 10A,C and Video 14.

claim: The two duplicated centrosomes exhibited equivalent motility in the cells with the omni-directional invaginations, in contrast to the asymmetric centrosome migration found in the cells displaying directional invaginations.
source: Following this, the two duplicated centrosomes exhibited equivalent motility in the cells with the omni-directional invaginations (Figure 10A; Omni-directional 105', Figure 10D and Video 14), in contrast to the asymmetric centrosome migration found in the cells displaying directional invaginations (Figure 10A; Directional 83', Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of centrosome migration shown in Figure 10A,D and Video 14.

claim: Epidermal cilia form in the center of the cells with omni-directional invaginations, instead of at a posterior position.
source: Finally, epidermal cilia form in the center of the cells with omni-directional invaginations, instead of at a posterior position (Figure 10E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 10E,F.

claim: The centrosome dynamics in ascidian epidermal cells is tightly correlated with the direction of membrane invaginations.
source: These results suggest that the centrosome dynamics in ascidian epidermal cells is tightly correlated with the direction of membrane invaginations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective observations showing that disruption of directional invaginations affects centrosome positioning, migration, and cilium localization.

claim: An unusual membrane structure, which forms during interphase of a specific embryonic cell cycle, is correlated with the dynamics of centrosomes including positioning of centrosomes and cilia and determination of the cell division axis.
source: We report here that an unusual membrane structure, which forms during interphase of a specific embryonic cell cycle, is correlated with the dynamics of centrosomes. This includes positioning of centrosomes and cilia and determination of the cell division axis (graphical summary and model in Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is a summary claim synthesizing the main findings of the study.

claim: The centrosome is captured by a unique membrane structure and is subsequently tethered to the posterior side of cells.
source: We propose a model whereby these events are coupled by physical interaction between a centriole and plasma membrane, which results in the generation of a tensile force in the latter. Although we could not directly demonstrate that the membrane invagination is required for mitotic spindle orientation, our data is consistent with our model whereby the centrosome is captured by a unique membrane structure and is subsequently tethered to the posterior side of cells.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective data, though the authors acknowledge they could not directly demonstrate causality.

claim: In the Drosophila stem cell systems, duplicated centrosomes generated from an eccentrically positioned centrosome show differential motilities.
source: In the Drosophila stem cell systems, duplicated centrosomes generated from an eccentrically positioned centrosome show differential motilities (Yamashita and Fuller, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the ascidian epidermal cells in the 11th cell cycle, the duplicated centrosomes exhibit differential motilities with the less motile centrosome remaining associated with the membrane invagination.
source: In the ascidian epidermal cells in the 11th cell cycle, the duplicated centrosomes also exhibit differential motilities with the less motile centrosome remaining associated with the membrane invagination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative data on centrosome migration presented in the manuscript.

claim: The formation of the ascidian membrane invagination, like the MT-nanotubes in Drosophila male germ cells, depends on microtubule function.
source: Although some microtubule (MT)-filled nanotubes resist nocodazole treatment (Önfelt et al., 2006), the formation of the ascidian membrane invagination, like the MT-nanotubes in Drosophila male germ cells (Inaba et al., 2015b), depends on microtubule function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the nocodazole treatment data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The distribution of the microtubule is distinct in ascidian invaginations versus Drosophila MT-nanotubes.
source: However, the distribution of the microtubule is distinct in the latter two tubular membrane structures and it is not known whether MT-nanotubes protrude toward the centrosome.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the authors' observations with the structure of MT-nanotubes described in literature.

claim: A similar membrane invagination to the one observed in ascidian embryos was previously reported in the C. elegans zygote.
source: Interestingly, a similar membrane invagination to the one we observed in ascidian embryos was previously reported in the C. elegans zygote, and it was suggested that the actomyosin cortex counteracts pulling forces mediated by microtubules, resulting in the posterior displacement of the spindle and the unequal cell division (Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological tests with either microtubule or actin inhibitors resulted in similar observations to those described for the C. elegans membrane invagination.
source: Our pharmacological tests with either microtubule or actin inhibitors resulted in similar observations to those described for the C. elegans membrane invagination.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the authors' experimental results with those reported for C. elegans.

claim: Membrane invaginations take place in normal (untreated) cells in a multicellular tissue (ascidian embryonic epidermis).
source: Importantly, we report here for the first time that membrane invaginations take place in normal (untreated) cells in a multicellular tissue (ascidian embryonic epidermis).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' observations in untreated ascidian embryos.

claim: These invaginations (generally one or two per cell) arising from two adjacent plasma membranes may control centrosome dynamics and the orientation of the cell division axis.
source: Our observations collectively indicate that these invaginations (generally one or two per cell) arising from two adjacent plasma membranes may control centrosome dynamics and the orientation of the cell division axis.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the collective observations, stated with appropriate caution ('may control').

claim: A similar membrane invagination is observed during the formation of immunological synapses between T cells and antigen-presenting cells.
source: It should be also noted that a similar membrane invagination is observed during the formation of immunological synapses between T cells and antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about immunological synapses.

claim: During immunological synapse formation, T cells rapidly reposition their centrosome to the center of the immunological synapse, and the centrosome repositioning is coupled with the formation of a membrane invagination originating from the synaptic interphase and reaching towards the T-cell centrosome in a mirotubule-dependent manner.
source: During this process, T cells rapidly reposition their centrosome to the center of the immunological synapse. Importantly, the centrosome repositioning is coupled with the formation of a membrane invagination originating from the synaptic interphase and reaching towards the T-cell centrosome in a mirotubule-dependent manner (Yi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The microtubule-dependent mechanism in which a membrane invagination captures and repositions the centrosome may be a general mechanism that transcends species and cell types for polarised centrosome repositioning.
source: Therefore, the microtubule-dependent mechanism in which a membrane invagination captures and repositions the centrosome may be a general mechanism that transcends species and cell types for polarised centrosome repositioning.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison of observations in ascidian embryos with those in T cells.

claim: In ascidian epidermal cells, the membrane invagination process appears to be also involved in the posterior positioning of the cilia.
source: In ascidian epidermal cells, this process appears to be also involved in the posterior positioning of the cilia.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cilia are associated with invaginations and that disruption of directional invaginations affects cilium positioning.

claim: The tip of the membrane invagination is found in close vicinity of the basal body, indicating that the membrane invagination might associate preferentially with the mother centriole.
source: In this study, we revealed that the tip of the membrane invagination is found in close vicinity of the basal body, indicating that the membrane invagination might associate preferentially with the mother centriole.
evidence: This claim is based on the distance measurements from SBF-SEM data.

claim: Specific molecules of the mother centriole might be involved in establishing the proposed association with the membrane invagination.
source: Since the mother and daughter centrioles inherit distinct components (Pelletier and Yamashita, 2012; Pereira et al., 2001), specific molecules of the mother centriole might be involved in establishing the proposed association with the membrane invagination.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on known differences between mother and daughter centrioles and the observed preferential association.

claim: Posteriorly localized cilia are found in several systems.
source: Posteriorly localized cilia are found in several systems and it will be interesting to determine if their position depends on similar mechanism (Antic et al., 2010; Borovina et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2010; Momose et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the initial length of the membrane invagination and both the average and maximum speed of regression following laser ablation.
source: In this study, we found the positive correlation between the initial length of the membrane invagination and both the average and maximum speed of regression following laser ablation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laser ablation experiments.

claim: The membrane invagination has an elastic restoring force rather than an active force generator like cell-cell junctions.
source: This observation implies that the membrane invagination has an elastic restoring force rather than an active force generator like cell-cell junctions (Ishihara and Sugimura, 2012; Rauzi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between initial length and recoil speed, compared with behavior of cell-cell junctions described in cited literature.

claim: The generation of membrane invaginations in C. elegans one-cell embryos involves cortical dynein motors.
source: Indeed, the generation of membrane invaginations in C. elegans one-cell embryos involves cortical dynein motors (Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A plus-end-directed motor protein would be one of the promising candidates for the formation of invagination in ascidian epidermal cells.
source: The microtubule-dependent invagination process targeting the centrosome implies the involvement of plus-end-directed motor. Indeed, the generation of membrane invaginations in C. elegans one-cell embryos involves cortical dynein motors (Redemann et al., 2010). Therefore, this plus-end motor protein would be one of the promising candidates for the formation of invagination in ascidian epidermal cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the microtubule-dependence of invagination formation and comparison with C. elegans.

claim: By disrupting a core PCP component in ascidian epidermal cells, there is a tight correlation between the direction of membrane invagination and centrosome dynamics including mitotic spindle orientation.
source: Furthermore, by disrupting a core PCP component in ascidian epidermal cells, we have shown a tight correlation between the direction of membrane invagination and centrosome dynamics including mitotic spindle orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Dsh knockdown experiments.

claim: In the Dsh knockdown experiment, the possibility that the PCP pathway affects centrosome behavior independently of the membrane structure cannot be ruled out.
source: However, in this experiment, we cannot rule out the possibility that the PCP pathway affects centrosome behavior independently of this membrane structure.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the Dsh knockdown results.
